findings.comment: Inspector observed the walk-in cooler fail to maintain proper cooling temperatures during today’s inspection. Ensure that the PIC is monitoring cold holding temperatures and preventing improper cold holding in the facility. A follow-up will be conducted on August 11th to ensure the cooler is being properly monitored.

findings.title: Proper cold holding temperatures.
findings.comment:
Inspector observed the following food items to be above the maximum safe cold holding temperature in the walk-in cooler (all probed):
1. Chili (50.8F)
2. Two large containers of raw chicken (50.8F)
4. Taco meat (48.7F)

CORRECTED: Inspector waited at facility and confirmed that walk-in cooler reached safe cold-holding temperatures relatively quickly. PIC stated that the door of the cooler was open for an extended period during food prep. Ensure the door remains closed as much as possible to ensure proper cold holding. Discussed maintaining cooler temperature logs to aid in temperature monitoring.

findings.citation_text: 3-302.11(A)(2) Packaged and Unpackaged Food - Separation, Packaging, and Segregation. (A) FOOD shall be protected from cross contamination by: (2) Except when combined as ingredients, separating types of raw animal FOODS from each other such as beef, FISH, lamb, pork, and POULTRY during storage, preparation, holding, and display by: (a) Using separate EQUIPMENT for each type, or (b) Arranging each type of FOOD in EQUIPMENT so that cross contamination of one type with another is prevented, and (c) Preparing each type of FOOD at different times or in separate areas.

A chemical SANITIZER used in a SANITIZING solution for a manual or mechanical operation at contact times specified under 4-703.11(C) shall meet the criteria specified under §7-204.11 Sanitizers, Criteria, shall be used in accordance with the EPA-registered label use instructions, and shall be used as follows: (C) A quaternary ammonium compound solution shall: (1) Have a minimum temperature of 24°C (75°F), (2) Have a concentration as specified under § 7-204.11 and as indicated by the manufacturer's use directions included in the labeling, and (3) Be used only in water with 500 MG/L hardness or less or in water having a hardness no greater than specified by the EPA-registered label use instructions.

findings.title: Proper date marking and disposition.
findings.comment: Observed chili in the walk-in cooler to bear a date exceeding 7 days (marked 4/6). The chili was actively in use in a warmer for service. Date marking practices will be spot checked during the follow-up scheduled for April 25th.
findings.citation_text: 3-501.18(A) Ready-to-Eat, Time/Temperature Control for Safety Food, Disposition. (A) A FOOD specified in 3-501.17(A) or (B) shall be discarded if it: (1) Exceeds the temperature and time combination specified in 3-501.17(A), except time that the product is frozen; (2) Is in a container or PACKAGE that does not bear a date or day; or (3) Is inappropriately marked with a date or day that exceeds a temperature and time combination as specified in 3-501.17(A).

findings.title: Proper date marking and disposition.
findings.comment: Observed cut tomatoes and cut lettuce in the prep cooler bottom to be missing appropriate date marks. Cut tomato and cut lettuce are considered time/temperature control for safety (TCS) foods. TCS foods must be marked with a date mark if stored longer than 24 hours after preparation and discarded after 7 days. A follow-up will be conducted on May 2nd to ensure compliance.
findings.citation_text: 3-501.17(A) Ready-to-Eat, Time/Temperature Control for Safety Food, Date Marking. (A) Except when PACKAGING FOOD using a REDUCED OXYGEN PACKAGING method as specified under § 3-502.12, and except as specified in (E) and (F) of this section, refrigerated, READY-TO-EAT, TIME/TEMPERATURE CONTROL FOR SAFETY FOOD prepared and held in a FOOD ESTABLISHMENT for more than 24 hours shall be clearly marked to indicate the date or day by which the FOOD shall be consumed on the PREMISES, sold, or discarded when held at a temperature of 5C (41F) or less for a maximum of 7 days. The day of preparation shall be counted as Day 1.

findings.title: Approved thawing methods used.
findings.comment: Observed bags of raw chicken thawing in the triple sink. The faucet was on over the thawing chicken, but the drip was inadequate to agitate and float off loose particles. PIC was informed that thawing methods were inadequate, and the water pressure was increased from the faucet. Ensure proper thawing methods are utilized to prevent the accumulation of bacteria in the chicken, resulting in food-borne illness. Thawing methods will be spot checked during the follow-up conducted on April 25th.
findings.citation_text: 3-501.13(B) Thawing. Except as specified in (D) of this section, TIME/TEMPERATURE CONTROL FOR SAFETY FOOD shall be thawed: (B) Completely submerged under running water: (1) At a water temperature of 21°C (70°F) or below, (2) With sufficient water velocity to agitate and float off loose particles in an overflow, and (3) For a period of time that does not allow thawed portions of READY-TO-EAT FOOD to rise above 5°C (41°F), or (4) For a period of time that does not allow thawed portions of a raw animal FOOD requiring cooking as specified under 3-401.11(A) or (B) to be above 5°C (41°F), for more than 4 hours including: (a) The time the FOOD is exposed to the running water and the time needed for preparation for cooking, or (b) The time it takes under refrigeration to lower the FOOD temperature to 5°C (41°F).

findings.title: Cold food at proper temperatures during storage, display, service, transport, and cold holding
findings.comment:
A) 750.120 - Beans in walkin cooler had internal temperature of 46F. A burger patty stacked above the fill line of a container in the top holding area of the prep cooler had surface and internal temperatures of 50F and 46F respectively. findings.title: Foods properly cooled
findings.citation_text:
750.140 - Mashed potatoes prepared late last night (around midnight) were observed to have surface temperatures well above 41F. Internal temperature of mashed potatoes stored in a plastic bowl was 53F, while the internal temperature of mashed potatoes stored in a metal container full to the top was 55F. Cook noted the potatoes were placed directly in the cooler after being made. Heavy condensation was observed on the inner surface of the plastic wrap used to cover the bowl of potatoes, and puddling condensation was also present in the product. The bowl of mashed potatoes was stacked on top of the metal container with potatoes full to the top. Mashed potatoes did not cool properly and were discarded in the trash during inspection.

Cooked potentially hazardous foods shall be properly cooled from 135F to 70F w/in 2 hrs and from 70F to 41F/below w/in an additional 4 hrs. Total cooling time must not exceed 6hrs. Time and temperature for cooling foods must be monitored to ensure foods are reaching benchmark temperatures in the designated time frame for proper cooling. Use a clean, calibrated stem thermometer to monitor temperature of foods during cooling process. Do not stack large quantities in containers on top of each other while products are cooling because this holds heat w/in the products, especially for thicker foods. Also, it is ok to leave containers of cooling foods uncovered as long as they are stored in a location within the cooler that does not pose a potential risk of cross contamination (i.e. on top shelf above all other foods). Place products in smaller portions and utilize ice baths to help rapidly cool foods to 41F/below prior to storing in larger quantities for long term storage.
**NOTE: Mashed potatoes were stored in the same area as the beans that were observed at 46F (see #3a). It is possible the heat from the cooling mashed potatoes affected temperatures of foods in other containers around the potatoes. Do not place hot foods directly in coolers. Utilize ice baths to help drop temperatures before putting foods in coolers**

Coolers are meant to hold cold food at 41F/below and not meant to cool hot foods. Utilize ice baths and separate foods into smaller portions to speed up the cooling process.
